cards.title: Introduction to Java Collections
cards.content:
The Java Collections Framework (JCF) is a unified architecture for representing and manipulating collections. It allows you to manipulate collections independently of the details of their representation.

The core interfaces of JCF include:

  • Collection: The root interface of the hierarchy.
  • List: An ordered collection (sequence) that allows duplicates.
  • Set: A collection that contains no duplicate elements.
  • Queue: A collection designed for holding elements prior to processing (FIFO).

cards.title: The List Interface: ArrayList vs LinkedList
cards.content:
ArrayList is backed by a dynamically resizing array. It provides fast O(1) random access but slower O(n) insertions and deletions in the middle of the list due to shifting elements.

LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list. It provides slower O(n) random access (as it must traverse the nodes) but offers constant O(1) time insertions and deletions once the location is reached.

List<String> arrayList = new ArrayList<>();
List<String> linkedList = new LinkedList<>();

options.text: ArrayList is faster than LinkedList for random search access by index.
LinkedList is faster than ArrayList for random search access by index.
Both collections offer equal performance for indexing operations.

cards.title: The Set Interface and Implementations
cards.content:
A Set is a collection that cannot contain duplicate elements. There are three main general-purpose Set implementations:

  • HashSet: Stores elements in a hash table. It is the best-performing implementation but makes no guarantees concerning the iteration order.
  • LinkedHashSet: Maintains a doubly-linked list running through all of its entries, yielding insertion-order iteration.
  • TreeSet: Stores elements in a red-black tree. Elements are sorted according to their natural ordering or a custom Comparator.

cards.title: The Map Interface
cards.content:
A Map maps keys to values. A map cannot contain duplicate keys; each key can map to at most one value.

Key implementations include:

  • HashMap: Unordered, permits null keys and values.
  • LinkedHashMap: Iterates in insertion-order.
  • TreeMap: Sorted by keys, does not permit null keys.
Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
scores.put("Alice", 95);

cards.title: Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterators
cards.content:
Iterators in the Java Collections Framework can behave in two ways when the underlying collection is modified during iteration:

  • Fail-Fast: Throws ConcurrentModificationException immediately if the collection is structurally modified during iteration (e.g., ArrayList, HashSet).
  • Fail-Safe (Weakly Consistent): Works on a clone/copy of the collection or handles concurrent modifications without throwing an exception (e.g., CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap).
